newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus says no quarrel with Russia's Yeltsin.
newsitem.headline: Belarus says no quarrel with Russia's Yeltsin.

text.p: A top Belarussian official on Wednesday rejected suggestions that Russian leader Boris Yeltsin had chided President Alexander Lukashenko for his handling of a constitutional stand-off with parliament.

Vladimir Zametalin, Lukashenko's deputy chief of staff, accused Russian media of bias in reporting Yeltsin's appeal to Lukashenko to calm the dispute. Parliament opposes a November referendum called by the president on expanding his powers.
Zametalin said the letter sent by Yeltsin, in hospital awaiting heart surgery, had really intended to boost an April pact creating a "community" between the two neighbours.

"The president was yet again disappointed by biased Russian media coverage crisis and how they interpreted the letter from Yeltsin," Zametalin told Reuters. "Someone is orchestrating this campaign. The real aim of this letter was...to give a boost to the creation of the Russian-Belarussian community."

Lukashenko, a hardline advocate of union with Russia, has called the vote for November 7, anniversary of the Bolshevik revolution, on a new constitution he says will enable him to rule for 10 more years.
Parliament, its disparate factions recently united to oppose Lukashenko, has called its own vote for November 24 on a different constitution abolishing the post of president.
Minsk streets are flush with posters urging voters to take part in the president's plebiscite.
In his letter, Yeltsin urged Lukashenko to do "everything possible to remove differences with the parliament".
Lukashenko has made no comment on the appeal. His office issued a brief statement saying he "shares the view of Boris Yeltsin on maintaining stability and intends to do so by democratic means."
Yeltsin has distanced himself from Lukashenko since signing the "community" pact in April.
But Security chief Alexander Lebed and Moscow Mayor Yuri Luzhkov, both certain contenders in any new presidential race to succeed Yeltsin, have praised the Belarussian president.

Elected Belarus's first post-Soviet president in 1994, ago, Lukashenko has since suspended trade unions, shut down newspapers and put the brakes on market reform. Some 200 people were jailed for demonstrating against the "community" pact.
State radio reported on Wednesday that Western ambassadors had urged Belarussian authorities to ensure their legal right to secure access to state officials and the media.
It quoted First Deputy Foreign Minister Valery Tsepkalo as telling the ambassadors that Belarus was upholding the provisions of international conventions.
